## Paper

## Abstract

Europe has experienced abnormal warming over the recent decades. Model-based studies highlight that multi-centennial internal variability of the North Atlantic can strongly affect European temperatures. However, the limited availability of high-resolution proxy records has hindered observational assessment of the existence and amplitude of such variability in the real climate system. Here, we compile annual-to-decadal proxy-based Holocene reconstructions, instrumental observations, and climate model simulations to demonstrate the existence of this multi-centennial variability mode and quantify its amplitude. We show that this mode is closely tied to the internal variability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. Its temporal evolution explains part of the observed 20th century variability, and a shift towards a positive phase in the late 1990s can explain the recent amplified warming over Europe. When its amplitude is constrained by observations, this internal variability may enhance anthropogenic warming in Northern Europe by up to 30% over 2000–2035.

---

## Introduction

During the 20th century, European summer temperature depicts a warming trend during the first 40 years1, followed by a cooling trend until the late 1970s2. Since the 1980s, Europe’s temperature has risen rapidly, becoming the fastest-warming continent on Earth, as highlighted in the European State of the Climate 2023 report from Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). However, most of the state-of-the-art General Circulation Models (GCM) simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) tend to underestimate the warming and heat extremes in Europe compared to recent observations3–6. As shown in Fig. 1a, b, recent trends in annual temperature over Europe are higher than the global average, and the observed temperature anomalies (compared to 1851–1900) clearly surpass the CMIP6 ensemble mean since the beginning of the last century (Fig. 1a, c). This is consistent with previous studies showing that CMIP6 GCM simulations tend to underestimate the observed warming over France7. Recent regional studies associated this fact either with poor representation in CMIP6 models of the recent observed trends in atmospheric circulation in western Europe8, or with prescribing constant aerosol forcing in EURO-CORDEX models over Europe9, or with a poor estimate of long-term aerosol changes in EURO-CORDEX simulations for western-central Europe10. Here, we highlight that larger warming over Europe as compared to the CMIP6 ensemble mean is also true in winter and is even larger than in summer (Fig. 1d).

The role of internal climate variability in this greater warming over Europe has been poorly assessed so far. In this context, our study focuses on internal climate variability and its potential role in the pronounced European warming in recent decades. We focus on multi-centennial climate fluctuations, where research remains limited: the existence, magnitude, and mechanisms of such low-frequency variability are still poorly constrained, while there is still no clear consensus on the existence of such a low-frequency variability and its underlying drivers11–13. Using high-resolution proxy records and model simulations, we aim to quantify this slow variability and evaluate its contribution to regional warming.

Climate is actually influenced by internal variability, which stems from the complex, chaotic interactions among the various components of the climate system14. Internal variability interacts with the effects of anthropogenically-forced climate change, caused most notably by the increasing emissions of greenhouse gases since the Industrial Revolution. Although the global warming observed over the past century is primarily attributed to the increase in greenhouse gas concentration, historical and future simulations include a large uncertainty, especially at the continental scale15. For instance, it has been shown16 that over France, 50% of the uncertainty in the warming level by 2050 is due to internal climate variability, 38% to the uncertainties in the climate models used, and the remaining 12% to the greenhouse gas emissions scenarios chosen by human societies. The latter, therefore, represents quite a small fraction of uncertainty within this time horizon. By 2100, these proportions move to 8, 22, and 70% for internal variability, climate models, and greenhouse gas emissions, respectively. At smaller spatial scales, where climate tends to be more variable, the contribution of internal variability to the uncertainty by 2100 can be dominant17. Understanding the magnitude and underlying mechanisms of internal variability is therefore essential for improving regional climate projections17.

In addition to the large uncertainty related to internal climate variability, recent modelling results have highlighted that atmospheric circulation might not sufficiently respond to changes in its boundary conditions, such as the ocean and sea ice (e.g. ref. 18). This important finding suggests that ocean variability could have a greater impact on the atmosphere than currently simulated by existing climate models. The variability over land related to the ocean could be therefore underestimated by climate models19, as a result of the so-called signal-to-noise paradox20. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), a key driver of heat transport in the North Atlantic, has shown internal centennial variability in some climate models that mirrors continental temperature shifts. This variability is reflected in the Atlantic Multi-decadal Variability (AMV), the dominant pattern of North Atlantic temperature fluctuations, highlighting a strong link between ocean circulation and regional climate patterns over Europe21,22. For example, Europe experiences widespread cooling when the AMOC is reduced23. Based on climate models simulations, ref. 13 suggested, that part of the global anthropogenic warming may have been obscured by a weakening of the AMOC during the second part of the 20th century24, which could be mainly associated with an internal multi-centennial variability mode. However, this variability was highly model-dependent, raising questions about its existence in the real world.

Given the short period of instrumental temperature data and the influence of the anthropogenic forcing during this period, it is not possible to provide an answer to these questions without longer observations of the past. To understand climate variability on multi-centennial timescales, long and high-resolution temperature reconstructions from palaeoclimate proxies and climate models are required. For this purpose, we focus here on the present interglacial period, the Holocene, over the last 6000 years. While other interglacial periods might also be relevant, the Holocene is well-documented in terms of temperature proxy data25, allowing for a more accurate reconstruction of past climates and providing a detailed backdrop for understanding low-frequency climate fluctuations. Additionally, advancements in climate modelling have allowed more refined models providing transient simulations over a large part of the Holocene26–28. While most proxy-model comparisons of palaeoclimate variability have been limited to the last millennium29, a too short period to estimate multi-centennial variability properly, a few recent studies have begun to use longer transient simulations11,30. Building on these advancements, we compare here various transient simulations, as well as available high-resolution (seasonal to decadal) palaeoclimate reconstructions of surface atmospheric temperature mainly over Europe25,31, covering the last 6000 years, and a recent proxy-based reanalysis covering the Holocene32 (see Methods). The aim of this study is to: (i) identify a common multi-centennial signal of natural climate variability across different palaeoclimate information sources and its origin; and (ii) deduce its potential impact on recent and near-future temperature trends in Europe.

---

## Results

Multi-centennial climate variability: a consistent signal across models, reconstructions, and Holocene reanalysis

Figure 2 compares the spectral density, significantly different from a red noise33, of temperature variations since the mid-Holocene, in proxy-based reconstructions (individual sites in Europe and Greenland; Fig. 2a and see Methods), transient climate models simulations and Holocene reanalysis data32 (over Europe; Fig. 2b), and simulated AMOC (Fig. 2c). The spectral analysis of low-pass filtered temperature data (see Methods) reveals significant periodicities (above the 99% significance level from the red noise) at the multi-centennial scales (~100–200 years) in most direct proxy reconstructions from diverse European sites, including the UK, the southwestern Norwegian continental margin, Sweden, and Finland. Comparable significant periodicities are also observed at a site in Greenland, although they can exceed 200 years, consistent with the findings of ref. 34. Similar spectral analyses have been conducted in transient simulations and in the Holocene reanalysis over Europe (Fig. 2b), in its northern (10°W–50°E, 55°N–70°N), central (10°W–50°E, 45°N–55°N) and southern sectors (10°W–50°E, 35°N–45°N) (Supplementary Figs. 1–3) showing similar peaks at multi-centennial timescales. This confirms that the multi-centennial-scale periodicity has a spatial signature that extends far beyond the individual sites where reconstructions are available and can be found over most of Europe. The consistency of this pattern across various models and European regions, as confirmed by reconstructions, suggests that processes at the multi-centennial scale might be a key driver of long-term climate variability. There are also smaller peaks in the spectral density, indicating multi-decadal variability at frequencies around 70 years, which can be related to the AMV35 mode.

The reanalysis (Supplementary Fig. 7) and the IPSL-CM6A-LR transient simulations (Supplementary Fig. 8) show patterns broadly consistent with those observed in the proxy records. These results indicate coherent multi-decadal to centennial variability across sites and suggest that the proxy records are primarily linked through common variability at these timescales, supporting the interpretation that they respond to large-scale climate phenomenon during specific Holocene intervals. While the simulations reproduce the timing and dominant spatial scales of common variability reasonably well, the amplitude of coherent variability is generally weaker in the reanalysis than in both the model simulations and the proxy records. The reanalysis likely underestimates real variability owing to limitations in spatial coverage, seasonal proxy sensitivities, temporal resolution, covariance-based infilling32, and low signal-to-noise ratios in proxy records36. In contrast, our work focuses specifically on Europe, a region where the impacts of variability and warming are especially strong.

Authors’ response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the phasing between regional proxy records. However, previous detailed studies7,17 have shown that in-phase variability across European proxies should not necessarily be expected. In fact, Sejrup et al.7 explicitly examined this issue using the same P1003 and Torneträsk records included in our study. Their spectral and multivariate analyses demonstrated that the dominant multi-centennial modes of variability vary in phase and amplitude through time and space. Bradley and Jones18 and Wanner et al.17 have also pointed out that some of the decadal to multi-centennial variability is not in phase between different archives/locations. This reflects the complex nature of North Atlantic climate variability, which arises from multiple, interacting mechanisms leading to leads and lags in the spatial response across Europe. It mirrors realistic regional differences in the propagation of large-scale ocean–atmosphere signals such as those associated with the AMOC and related teleconnections. These signals can influence different parts of Europe and the North Atlantic with variable timing and magnitude, depending on the structure of the events themselves and shifting background states.

Comment 2.7 (4) proxy uncertainties are not accounted for, but periodicity, amplitudes and significance of individual peaks might be sensitive to them.
Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We believe that the main sources of uncertainty in the selected proxy records are related to (i) potential seasonal biases, (ii) calibration to temperature, and (iii) age uncertainties. While the first two might not affect spectral analysis, we believe that the age uncertainty is not expected to be a significant issue, as the proxy records are annually resolved and based on annually constrained chronologies (tree rings and varved sediments). The reported age uncertainty primarily arises from cumulative counting errors and from uncertainties associated with other dating methods (e.g., radiocarbon or tephrochronology), when annual-layer chronologies are anchored to such dates. This uncertainty mainly affects the absolute age of a record or the dating of a specific event (e.g., a climate event occurring at 4.2 ± 0.3 kyr BP). Counting errors are typically quantified as the standard deviation among independent counts of annual layers (for example, in varve chronologies, at least three separate counts are commonly performed; see Ojala et al.19. Because both the tree-ring and varve records are annually resolved, we are also able to estimate counting errors for the duration of specific intervals, which are independent of cumulative counting errors (e.g., the Maunder Minimum lasted 70 ± 2 years).
The annual resolution of these chronologies allows us to perform time series analyses without temporal uncertainty affecting the periodicities themselves (e.g., tree-ring width = one data point per year). However, age uncertainty may slightly influence the absolute placement of these periodicities along the timescale. The only exception is the marine record included in this study, which has a temporal resolution of approximately 12 years according to its chronology. While this may introduce an uncertainty of ±12 years (on average)7 in the identified periodicities, such an error is negligible when considering variability at multi-centennial timescales.

Comment 2.13 Fig. 3: When low-pass filtering a <200-year time series with a 60-year filter, it becomes quite important how the “edges” (the first and last 60 years) of the time series are treated. Authors’ response: For the low-pass filtering, we applied a Butterworth filter that internally handles the treatment of the series edges. Specifically, it subtracts the mean of the input series and then pads the data at both ends by reflection to a length of twice the maximum period before applying the filter. This reflection padding is designed to minimize edge effects and avoid artifacts that would arise from simpler approaches such as zero-padding. After filtering, the function removes the padding and adds back the series mean. Thus, no explicit zero-padding was applied.
The use of reflection padding in combination with the forward–backward filtfilt algorithm ensures that phase distortions are removed and that unwanted artifacts at the edges are minimized.
We have now included this into the Method section in the revised manuscript:

This reflection padding is designed to minimize edge effects and avoid artifacts that would arise from simpler approaches such as zero-padding. Authors’ response: To estimate the red-noise spectra, we used the REDFIT program34, which applies the Lomb–Scargle periodogram and is specifically designed to handle unevenly spaced data such as paleoclimate records. REDFIT fits the time series to a simulated first-order autoregressive [AR(1)] process, which serves as the null hypothesis. However, because we use high-resolution (annual) time series spanning the Holocene, the raw data contain substantial high-frequency noise. This can cause the AR(1) model to fail for some series, preventing a valid fit. To address this, we applied a low-pass Butterworth filter to remove short-term fluctuations, thereby allowing REDFIT to reliably estimate the AR(1) process and avoid fitting errors. Since our study focuses on multi-centennial variability, filtering out the high-frequency component is both appropriate and necessary. The same procedure was applied uniformly to all proxy records and model simulations to ensure consistency during the pre-processing stage.

### Reviewer 2

I thank the authors for their thorough replies and revisions. I still have some concerns about the robustness of the model and proxy results, but they should not preclude publication. However, it would be good to include some additional analysis and slightly adapt the study’s overall framing.

Remaining concerns
1. Proxy record selection. In the previous round of reviews, two reviewers were concerned about the limited number of proxy records. The authors referred to Münch & Laepple (2018) and Grisart et al. (2022) to argue that “this kind of resolution (~ 10 years) is necessary”. I might have overread something, but I could not find any statement in these studies that would preclude the use of records at slightly lower resolution (say, 10 to 20 years) to assess (multi-)centennial variability. Furthermore, both studies seem to be specifically about ice cores.

One option would be to demonstrate more rigorously here why a specific minimum resolution would be needed regardless of proxy type. However, it might be easier to relax the resolution threshold a little and include some more records in the analysis, which would improve the robustness of the model-data comparison.

Even if the strict temporal resolution criteria are kept, the study currently does not include any ice records from the Temp12k database, e.g., from Greenland. I don’t see why they shouldn’t be included in an analysis of AMOC-related variability – even though these sites are not technically located in Europe, their temperatures should be expected to co-vary considerably with European temperatures at centennial timescales.

2. Phase relationship. The authors raise an interesting point with the Sejrup et al. (2011) study, in that it “demonstrated that the dominant multi-centennial modes of variability vary in phase and amplitude through time and space. (…) This reflects the complex nature of North Atlantic climate variability, which arises from multiple, interacting mechanisms leading to leads and lags in the spatial response across Europe”.

Models’ modes of variability at multidecadal and longer timescales often yield highly coherent temperature signals over and near the North Atlantic. For a fair model-data comparison, especially regarding the link to the AMOC, it would therefore be good to compare the spectral coherence of the proxy records at (multi-)centennial timescales to the coherence in the model. This is not necessarily the same as records being in phase (my previous comment might have been confusing in this regard); rather, that they have a coherent variability, potentially with a regional phase difference (e.g., related to shifts in deep convection).

3. Model-data comparison. From my understanding, arguments for the plausibility of the multi-centennial variability in the IPSL model are now mainly based on two approaches: comparison of temperature spectra with the Holocene reanalysis and the amplitude of modelled vs observed internal variability during the instrumental period. I still have some concerns regarding both approaches.

Regarding the observed internal variability, I respectfully disagree with the authors’ reply that it is appropriate to use the IPSL ensemble mean for this calculation. (Of course it is appropriate to subtract the IPSL ensemble mean to calculate the model’s own internal variability.) As mentioned in the previous review, the CMIP6 multi-model mean already used in Fig. R5 (or, even better, the residual of the multi-model mean regressed onto observations, https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.1257856) is a more appropriate proxy of the real-world forced response, from which the observed internal variability is calculated. I don’t expect this to change the results substantially, but it will probably change the percentages in Table 1.

Comparison with the Holocene reanalysis is so far mostly based on significant frequencies in the power spectra (Fig. 2), which match at least qualitatively. However, the amplitudes appear quite different, even with normalization but especially without. For example, judging from the color scale in Fig. S5, the spectral power of (multi-)centennial variability in the IPSL model seems about twice as large as in the reanalysis. How does this translate to an amplitude in °C? If there are indeed significant discrepancies in the amplitude, this should be acknowledged more clearly in the manuscript. Along these lines, Mehling et al. (2024) suggested that the amplitude of centennial AMOC variability in some NEMO-based models (including the IPSL model) might be overestimated due to a sea ice bias in the Labrador Sea.

Finally, the comparison of the models with the Holocene reanalysis would be more convincing if the spatial patterns of the centennial temperature variability were also compared, which is again relevant for the assumed link to the AMOC.

To summarize, I am still not convinced that there is enough evidence that the multi-centennial variability in the IPSL model is entirely realistic (or, on the other hand, that the variability in the other models is unrealistic, so that they shouldn’t be considered for the analysis of temperature trends). However, conclusions such as “this mode of variability is amplifying the warming induced by human activity in Northern Europe by 53% over the 2000-2035 period” (from the abstract) rely on the realism of variability in the IPSL model.

I think that this dilemma can be solved relatively easily by slightly adapting the overall framing: emphasizing the importance of multi-centennial (AMOC) variability for present-day European temperature trends while also emphasizing that discrepancies likely remain between modelled and observed/reconstructed variability, and acknowledging that centennial variability remains hard to evaluate (although this study has taken an important step in the right direction).

## Paper

## Abstract

Europe has experienced abnormal warming over the recent decades. Model-based studies highlight that multi-centennial internal variability of the North Atlantic can strongly affect European temperatures. However, the limited availability of high-resolution proxy records has hindered observational assessment of the existence and amplitude of such variability in the real climate system. Here, we compile annual-to-decadal proxy-based Holocene reconstructions, instrumental observations, and climate model simulations to demonstrate the existence of this multi-centennial variability mode and quantify its amplitude. We show that this mode is closely tied to the internal variability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. Its temporal evolution explains part of the observed 20th century variability, and a shift towards a positive phase in the late 1990s can explain the recent amplified warming over Europe. When its amplitude is constrained by observations, this internal variability may enhance anthropogenic warming in Northern Europe by up to 30% over 2000–2035.

---

## Introduction

During the 20th century, European summer temperature depicts a warming trend during the first 40 years1, followed by a cooling trend until the late 1970s2. Since the 1980s, Europe’s temperature has risen rapidly, becoming the fastest-warming continent on Earth, as highlighted in the European State of the Climate 2023 report from Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). However, most of the state-of-the-art General Circulation Models (GCM) simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) tend to underestimate the warming and heat extremes in Europe compared to recent observations3–6. As shown in Fig. 1a, b, recent trends in annual temperature over Europe are higher than the global average, and the observed temperature anomalies (compared to 1851–1900) clearly surpass the CMIP6 ensemble mean since the beginning of the last century (Fig. 1a, c). This is consistent with previous studies showing that CMIP6 GCM simulations tend to underestimate the observed warming over France7. Recent regional studies associated this fact either with poor representation in CMIP6 models of the recent observed trends in atmospheric circulation in western Europe8, or with prescribing constant aerosol forcing in EURO-CORDEX models over Europe9, or with a poor estimate of long-term aerosol changes in EURO-CORDEX simulations for western-central Europe10. Here, we highlight that larger warming over Europe as compared to the CMIP6 ensemble mean is also true in winter and is even larger than in summer (Fig. 1d).

The role of internal climate variability in this greater warming over Europe has been poorly assessed so far. In this context, our study focuses on internal climate variability and its potential role in the pronounced European warming in recent decades. We focus on multi-centennial climate fluctuations, where research remains limited: the existence, magnitude, and mechanisms of such low-frequency variability are still poorly constrained, while there is still no clear consensus on the existence of such a low-frequency variability and its underlying drivers11–13. Using high-resolution proxy records and model simulations, we aim to quantify this slow variability and evaluate its contribution to regional warming.

Climate is actually influenced by internal variability, which stems from the complex, chaotic interactions among the various components of the climate system14. Internal variability interacts with the effects of anthropogenically-forced climate change, caused most notably by the increasing emissions of greenhouse gases since the Industrial Revolution. Although the global warming observed over the past century is primarily attributed to the increase in greenhouse gas concentration, historical and future simulations include a large uncertainty, especially at the continental scale15. For instance, it has been shown16 that over France, 50% of the uncertainty in the warming level by 2050 is due to internal climate variability, 38% to the uncertainties in the climate models used, and the remaining 12% to the greenhouse gas emissions scenarios chosen by human societies. The latter, therefore, represents quite a small fraction of uncertainty within this time horizon. By 2100, these proportions move to 8, 22, and 70% for internal variability, climate models, and greenhouse gas emissions, respectively. At smaller spatial scales, where climate tends to be more variable, the contribution of internal variability to the uncertainty by 2100 can be dominant17. Understanding the magnitude and underlying mechanisms of internal variability is therefore essential for improving regional climate projections17.

In addition to the large uncertainty related to internal climate variability, recent modelling results have highlighted that atmospheric circulation might not sufficiently respond to changes in its boundary conditions, such as the ocean and sea ice (e.g. ref. 18). This important finding suggests that ocean variability could have a greater impact on the atmosphere than currently simulated by existing climate models. The variability over land related to the ocean could be therefore underestimated by climate models19, as a result of the so-called signal-to-noise paradox20. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), a key driver of heat transport in the North Atlantic, has shown internal centennial variability in some climate models that mirrors continental temperature shifts. This variability is reflected in the Atlantic Multi-decadal Variability (AMV), the dominant pattern of North Atlantic temperature fluctuations, highlighting a strong link between ocean circulation and regional climate patterns over Europe21,22. For example, Europe experiences widespread cooling when the AMOC is reduced23. Based on climate models simulations, ref. 13 suggested, that part of the global anthropogenic warming may have been obscured by a weakening of the AMOC during the second part of the 20th century24, which could be mainly associated with an internal multi-centennial variability mode. However, this variability was highly model-dependent, raising questions about its existence in the real world.

Given the short period of instrumental temperature data and the influence of the anthropogenic forcing during this period, it is not possible to provide an answer to these questions without longer observations of the past. To understand climate variability on multi-centennial timescales, long and high-resolution temperature reconstructions from palaeoclimate proxies and climate models are required. For this purpose, we focus here on the present interglacial period, the Holocene, over the last 6000 years. While other interglacial periods might also be relevant, the Holocene is well-documented in terms of temperature proxy data25, allowing for a more accurate reconstruction of past climates and providing a detailed backdrop for understanding low-frequency climate fluctuations. Additionally, advancements in climate modelling have allowed more refined models providing transient simulations over a large part of the Holocene26–28. While most proxy-model comparisons of palaeoclimate variability have been limited to the last millennium29, a too short period to estimate multi-centennial variability properly, a few recent studies have begun to use longer transient simulations11,30. Building on these advancements, we compare here various transient simulations, as well as available high-resolution (seasonal to decadal) palaeoclimate reconstructions of surface atmospheric temperature mainly over Europe25,31, covering the last 6000 years, and a recent proxy-based reanalysis covering the Holocene32 (see Methods). The aim of this study is to: (i) identify a common multi-centennial signal of natural climate variability across different palaeoclimate information sources and its origin; and (ii) deduce its potential impact on recent and near-future temperature trends in Europe.

---

## Results

Multi-centennial climate variability: a consistent signal across models, reconstructions, and Holocene reanalysis

Figure 2 compares the spectral density, significantly different from a red noise33, of temperature variations since the mid-Holocene, in proxy-based reconstructions (individual sites in Europe and Greenland; Fig. 2a and see Methods), transient climate models simulations and Holocene reanalysis data32 (over Europe; Fig. 2b), and simulated AMOC (Fig. 2c). The spectral analysis of low-pass filtered temperature data (see Methods) reveals significant periodicities (above the 99% significance level from the red noise) at the multi-centennial scales (~100–200 years) in most direct proxy reconstructions from diverse European sites, including the UK, the southwestern Norwegian continental margin, Sweden, and Finland. Comparable significant periodicities are also observed at a site in Greenland, although they can exceed 200 years, consistent with the findings of ref. 34. Similar spectral analyses have been conducted in transient simulations and in the Holocene reanalysis over Europe (Fig. 2b), in its northern (10°W–50°E, 55°N–70°N), central (10°W–50°E, 45°N–55°N) and southern sectors (10°W–50°E, 35°N–45°N) (Supplementary Figs. 1–3) showing similar peaks at multi-centennial timescales. This confirms that the multi-centennial-scale periodicity has a spatial signature that extends far beyond the individual sites where reconstructions are available and can be found over most of Europe. The consistency of this pattern across various models and European regions, as confirmed by reconstructions, suggests that processes at the multi-centennial scale might be a key driver of long-term climate variability. There are also smaller peaks in the spectral density, indicating multi-decadal variability at frequencies around 70 years, which can be related to the AMV35 mode.

Wavelet analysis (see Methods) reveals that most proxy records (Supplementary Fig. 4) exhibit multi-centennial-scale variability (~70–300 years), though its occurrence and intensity vary across records and time periods. Some proxies, such as the one from Lapland (tree-ring width), display more persistent variability, whereas others, like the one from Nautajärvi (lake sediment) and Diss Mere (lake sediment), show more intermittent signals. Wavelet analysis in the Holocene reanalysis and transient simulations over Europe (Supplementary Fig. 5) reveals a similar multi-centennial variability (~70–300 years). Furthermore, significant coherent spectral power is concentrated at multi-decadal to centennial timescales (~60–200 years) across most proxy pairs (Supplementary Fig. 6). At longer periods (>200 years), coherence occurs intermittently and varies among proxy pairs. The reanalysis (Supplementary Fig. 7) and the IPSL-CM6A-LR transient simulations (Supplementary Fig. 8) show patterns broadly consistent with those observed in the proxy records. These results indicate coherent multi-decadal to centennial variability across sites and suggest that the proxy records are primarily linked through common variability at these timescales, supporting the interpretation that they respond to large-scale climate phenomenon during specific Holocene intervals. While the simulations reproduce the timing and dominant spatial scales of common variability reasonably well, the amplitude of coherent variability is generally weaker in the reanalysis than in both the model simulations and the proxy records. When quantified in temperature units, IPSL-CM6A-LR exhibits larger amplitudes than the reanalysis across all regions, with model-to-reanalysis standard deviation ratios of ~4–6 (Supplementary Table S2). In contrast, comparisons between IPSL-CM6A-LR simulations and proxy records yield lower ratios, mostly between ~1 and 4, indicating a more moderate model overestimation relative to proxies. This implies that IPSL-CM6A-LR provides an upper-end estimate of low-frequency temperature variability, rather than a conservative one. Indeed, the Holocene reanalysis itself also shows reduced variability compared to those proxy records (Supplementary Table S2). The reanalysis likely underestimates real variability owing to limitations in spatial coverage, seasonal proxy sensitivities, temporal resolution, covariance-based infilling32, and low signal-to-noise ratios in proxy records36. All those limitations might lead to a damping in the amplitude of the variations in the reanalysis.

Former studies13,37 have suggested that the multi-centennial temperature variability was linked to a low-frequency mode of the AMOC in climate models. Mehling et al.38, for instance, analysed AMOC variability in pre-industrial control simulations (piControl) from nine CMIP6 models and found that six models exhibited a statistically significant mode of multi-centennial variability. Similar multi-centennial variability was also evident in the piControl of the IPSL-CM6A-LR13 and EC-Earth39 climate models, indicating that this mode might be primarily driven by internal dynamics rather than external forcing over the Holocene. Here, we also identify a multi-centennial AMOC variability (~100–200 years) in the transient model simulations since the mid-Holocene (Fig. 2c), with periodicities (Supplementary Fig. 9) similar to those found in European temperature reconstructions (Supplementary Fig. 4) and transient simulations over Europe (Supplementary Fig. 5). Moreover, a wavelet coherence analysis of transient simulations reveals that the AMOC and European temperature are in phase (Supplementary Fig. 10), exhibiting persistent coherence in the multi-centennial variability mode during the last six thousand years. These results reinforce the hypothesis that multi-centennial variability is an inherent feature of the coupled ocean-atmosphere system driven primarily by the AMOC. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript focuses on internal climate variability and highlights the significant impact of multi-centennial variability in the North Atlantic (AMOC) on European temperatures. It argues that up to 50% of the uncertainty in climate model projections of future warming is attributable to internal variability, which remains poorly understood. The manuscript further emphasizes that understanding the magnitude and underlying mechanisms of this variability is essential for improving the accuracy of regional climate predictions. The authors also flag an issue with atmospheric circulation, which might not sufficiently respond to changes in its boundary conditions.

The manuscript is interesting and well written. The topic is relevant for a broad community and noteworthy.
However, I have a main concern regarding the use of the proxy records (I am not a climate modeler, so I would recommend that someone with such a background evaluate the methods).

The authors focus on proxy records from the Holocene, where a great amount of data already exists. However, the selected sites/records are not from regions where the discrepancy between the data and the model is the largest—I wonder why? What was the rationale for selecting these sites? I think this should be mentioned. Why are they mainly covering Northern Europe? Will the conclusions based on this dataset be unbiased, given that it does not represent a broader spatial coverage?

This leads to another issue: why compare different proxies? My main concern is that the differences in the records may be related to the different methods/proxies applied (e.g., tree rings vs. lake deposits), and not necessarily to the frequency mode of AMOC. How do these two systems respond to temperature change? What is their sensitivity to detecting changes in temperature? Will both tree rings and lake deposits be able to detect the same frequencies of temperature changes? This is quite crucial, but the authors seem to ignore that every proxy has its limitations and uncertainties. Without addressing these issues at the proxy level, any further conclusions are speculative. If there is indeed so much data available from the Holocene (line 128), why not focus on the same archive and spread the sites across Europe?

And my last point: what is the temporal resolution of these records?

Minor points:
Line 71: “where research remains limited,” – what authors means by this?
Line 75: why capital letters here “Time Evolution of Global and European surface temperature Anomalies.”
Line 113: I think that while introduction of AMOC is OK here, I would suggest to introduce AMV since this the pattern of temperature fluctuations which is in focus of this paper.
Lines 122-139 – it is not really clear which proxy data authors are using (mention either instrumental data or proxy data). Earlier they mention e.g. temperatures (line 115) and refer also to a paper (ref.26) on temperatures. I think that clarification will make that section less vague.

### Reviewer 2

This study assesses the role of (multi-)centennial climate variability on recent and near-future temperature trends over Europe. It is shown that temperature variability on these timescales linked to the AMOC is quite common in paleoclimate proxies and transient climate model simulations. Then, one member from a single climate model ensemble, which appears to match European temperatures over the instrumental period, is used to analyze which phase of low-frequency variability was realized in the real world. The authors conclude that this particular realization of internal variability amplifies recent and near-future European temperature trends.

While this study sets out with an interesting and ambitious research question, it is not convincing that the methods used (especially the use of one simulation of only one climate model) yield robust results. The paleoclimate model/data comparison also misses some steps to show that there is indeed a robust mode of multi-centennial variability during the Holocene. It might be possible to address these shortcomings, but this might change the conclusions. Therefore, I recommend resubmitting this manuscript only after substantial revisions.

Additionally, it remains unclear how the approach and results here differ from the previous model/data comparison of multi-centennial variability by Askjaer et al. 2022 (ref. 9) as well as from the analysis by Bonnet et al. 2021 (ref. 11), who used the same single-model ensemble for a very similar research question regarding near-term temperature projections.

Major comments
Use of only one climate model.
The main findings of this paper depend sensitively on the realism of simulated multi-centennial variability in a single climate model, which is known to have a quite strong multi-centennial (AMOC) variability. In CMIP6, more than a dozen models now provide (large) ensemble simulations of the historical period (cf. Maher et al. 2024 and https://www.cesm.ucar.edu/community-projects/mmlea/v1) and the simulated amplitudes of (low-frequency) variability differ widely.

Because there are no (paleoclimate) constraints that would show that the IPSL model is the only one with realistic internal variability, the analysis of recent/near-future changes should include historical ensembles of as many models as possible (or as many as possible which meet some paleoclimate constraints) – only then, the impact of internal variability can be robustly assessed.

In addition, I don’t think that choosing a single ensemble member that (visually?) matches the observations best is an adequate way of constraining the ensemble – a certain degree of uncertainty should be accounted for, for example by using a weighted mean of several ensemble members according to their RMSE with observations.

Model-data comparison.
From my understanding, this comparison should mainly lend credibility to the multi-centennial mode of variability in the IPSL model which is later used to assess temperature trends. However, I am not convinced that it does so entirely since
(1) the spectral analysis of individual proxies currently does not show a coherent “mode of variability” (L343). For this, the phasing of the variability between different records would need to be verified (the European records should be more or less in phase, also with the AMOC reconstruction)
(2) the dominant period in the IPSL model (around 200 years from Fig. 2b and Jiang et al. 2021, ref. 36) is not very well-represented in the proxy data;
(3) as far as I can see, the amplitude of multi-centennial variability in the IPSL model (and other models) is not quantitatively evaluated, although this is promised in the abstract (L34);

Comment 2.7 (4) proxy uncertainties are not accounted for, but periodicity, amplitudes and significance of individual peaks might be sensitive to them.
Authors’ response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We believe that the main sources of uncertainty in the selected proxy records are related to (i) potential seasonal biases, (ii) calibration to temperature, and (iii) age uncertainties. While the first two might not affect spectral analysis, we believe that the age uncertainty is not expected to be a significant issue, as the proxy records are annually resolved and based on annually constrained chronologies (tree rings and varved sediments). The reported age uncertainty primarily arises from cumulative counting errors and from uncertainties associated with other dating methods (e.g., radiocarbon or tephrochronology), when annual-layer chronologies are anchored to such dates. This uncertainty mainly affects the absolute age of a record or the dating of a specific event (e.g., a climate event occurring at 4.2 ± 0.3 kyr BP). Counting errors are typically quantified as the standard deviation among independent counts of annual layers (for example, in varve chronologies, at least three separate counts are commonly performed; see Ojala et al.19. Because both the tree-ring and varve records are annually resolved, we are also able to estimate counting errors for the duration of specific intervals, which are independent of cumulative counting errors (e.g., the Maunder Minimum lasted 70 ± 2 years).
The annual resolution of these chronologies allows us to perform time series analyses without temporal uncertainty affecting the periodicities themselves (e.g., tree-ring width = one data point per year). However, age uncertainty may slightly influence the absolute placement of these periodicities along the timescale. The only exception is the marine record included in this study, which has a temporal resolution of approximately 12 years according to its chronology. While this may introduce an uncertainty of ±12 years (on average)7 in the identified periodicities, such an error is negligible when considering variability at multi-centennial timescales.

Authors’ response: For the low-pass filtering, we applied a Butterworth filter that internally handles the treatment of the series edges. Specifically, it subtracts the mean of the input series and then pads the data at both ends by reflection to a length of twice the maximum period before applying the filter. After filtering, the function removes the padding and adds back the series mean. Thus, no explicit zero-padding was applied.

However, because we use high-resolution (annual) time series spanning the Holocene, the raw data contain substantial high-frequency noise. This can cause the AR(1) model to fail for some series, preventing a valid fit. To address this, we applied a low-pass Butterworth filter to remove short-term fluctuations, thereby allowing REDFIT to reliably estimate the AR(1) process and avoid fitting errors. Since our study focuses on multi-centennial variability, filtering out the high-frequency component is both appropriate and necessary. The same procedure was applied uniformly to all proxy records and model simulations to ensure consistency during the pre-processing stage.
